questions.prompt: Write the remote hands request. Assume the replacement disk is already on site. Include everything their technician needs to do the job correctly on the first attempt, and say what you want them to report back.
questions.answer: Subject: failed disk replacement, Basic Info: site location, cage, rack, server (hostname), priority, Objective: the replacement disk is already on site, pls physically identify the failed disk in the specified server, and replace it with the provided disk, IMPORTANT: do not remove or replace any other disk, the SN of the failed disk must be vefified before removal, Before Installation: record replacement disk SN, model and capacity, confirm that the replacement is physically compatible with the server and match the required drive type/form factor before installation, Procedure: provide the detailed procedures for the technician, Report Back: server hostname, service tag, info of the failed drive removed (SN, Bay, Model, Capacity), info of the replacement drive (same with the failed drive), replacement drive seated successfully (yes/no), drive LED state after the installation, server power state, alarms/LEDs/physical damage, photographs of the server and the drives affected

questions.prompt: Write the handover note you would leave on the ticket: what you did, where things stand now, what is still outstanding, and what you would do next. Five to ten sentences.
questions.answer: The failed disk in Task 1 was replaced successfully, using the drive serial number to identify the correct disk, and the replacement is now installed in the original bay. The server was left powered on and no other drives or hardware were disturbed. Task 2 remains outstanding: the affected multipath device mpathg still has only one visible path, sdg, while the other comparable multipath devices have two paths. The affected path is associated with WWID 35000c500e1a4b107; the underlying device is sdg. The next technician should verify the physical connectivity and storage path for the missing second path, including cabling/HBA/target visibility and the storage-side presentation if applicable. After correcting the underlying path issue, recheck multipath -ll and confirm that mpathg has the expected number of healthy paths. Also verify the replacement disk and storage system health after recovery. Do not close the ticket until the multipath path issue is resolved and the storage environment is confirmed healthy

questions.prompt: On a standard Linux system, how are user passwords stored in /etc/shadow? Answer with a single letter.
Why is it done that way rather than the other way? Two or three sentences.
questions.answer: Passwords are stored as hashes so the system can verify a password without needing to decrypt and recover the original. A unique salt makes identical passwords produce different stored values and makes attacks much harder.

questions.prompt: A server accepts SSH connections with a username and password. What, if anything, would you change to bring it in line with good practice, and why?
questions.answer: I would disable username/password auth and enable public-key auth instead, SSH keys provide strong cryptographic auth without transmitting the password for auth, and they can be individually managed or revoked, additionally, we can use passphrase to protect the private key on a host, using this way, we can secure the system by 2 methods: something we have (private key) and something we know (the passphrase), even if someone can steal our private key, they cannot use it for auth without knowing the passphrase

questions.prompt: What separates a good monitor or alert from a bad one? Describe the qualities a good one has, and what makes a bad one worse than no alert at all.
questions.answer: A good alert is actionable: it detects a real problem, tells you what is affected, gives enough context to investigate, and reaches the right person at the right time. It should have a clear threshold, avoid unnecessary duplicates, and ideally include useful information such as the host, service, symptom, and when the problem started. A bad alert is noisy, vague, or not actionable—for example, alerting every time CPU briefly reaches 80% without any evidence of impact. Too many false positives cause alert fatigue, where people start ignoring alerts, which can make a bad alert worse than no alert at all because an important alert can get lost among the noise.

questions.prompt: During an outage, what do you think is the hardest part of handling it? And once service is restored, what still needs to happen?
questions.answer: The hardest part during an outage is staying organized while identifying the root cause, because multiple symptoms can appear at once and it is easy to make unnecessary changes that complicate the problem. Clear communication and prioritizing service restoration are also important. Once service is restored, I would verify that the system is fully healthy, continue monitoring it, document the timeline and actions taken, and determine the root cause. Any underlying issues found during the incident should be addressed, and monitoring or procedures should be improved to help prevent the same outage from happening again
